tagline: From a Quaker village to Short Creek and the Ohio River
intro: At Connorville, State Route 150 follows the southern edge of a community in the Short Creek valley. Rayland lies 1.5 miles east, where the creek reaches the Ohio River.

Mount Pleasant’s history centers on organized opposition to slavery. Quaker residents published antislavery literature, sheltered people escaping slavery and established a school for free Black children. A Free Produce Store followed in 1848, refusing goods made with enslaved labor. After the Civil War, railroads bypassed the village and its economy stagnated.

Begin in Mount Pleasant, whose original street and lot plan survives at Union and Concord streets. Continue east through Connorville toward Rayland, where the Short Creek valley reaches the Ohio River.

moments.title: Benjamin Lundy House
moments.text: A brick house at Union and Market streets connects abolitionist publishing with the choices people made at a store counter. Benjamin Lundy lived here for one year and began publishing The Genius of Universal Emancipation during his residence. The building also served as an Underground Railroad station and housed a free produce store, which rejected products and profits tied to enslaved labor. The house stands at an angle to Union Street, with a gabled roof and a recessed extension beside its main section. Ohio History Connection acquired the house in 2015 and stabilized it.
moments.notice: Look for the brick house’s gabled roof and recessed extension.

moments.title: Connorville
moments.text: Short Creek gives Connorville its valley setting and a connection east to the Ohio River at Rayland. State Route 150 runs along the community’s southern side, linking Dillonvale to the west with Rayland to the east. A coal mine here once employed 60 men. A country store and a post office also served the community; the post office operated from 1899 to 1958.

moments.title: Rayland
moments.text: Rayland carried a different name when its post office opened in 1871: Portland Station. The Ohio River village became Rayland in 1928 and incorporated in 1938. One of its lost landmarks was the Stringer Stone House, built in 1836 by Maryland abolitionist John Brown Bayless. The three-and-a-half-story gray sandstone house had its main entrances on the second story and faced away from the road. Inside, murals included a waterfall beside the stairs and a scene of a gristmill and its workers. Jefferson D. Stringer bought the house in 1860. Fire destroyed it in 1982.
